124-deuterocanonical-books-of-the-bible-:
Some Bibles include books that others set apart, and this volume gathers them. The Deuterocanonical Books, also called the Apocrypha, include Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, and Baruch. Esdras, the additions to Esther and Daniel, and the Maccabees books appear as well.

These writings come from the centuries between the Testaments, in Greek and Hebrew traditions. They tell of exiles, martyrs, wise sayings, and revolts for the faith. Churches differ on their authority, but all value their history. The collection gives readers the full disputed shelf in one place. Study notes in many editions explain where each book fits in Jewish and Christian history.
15571-mary-cary-frequently-martha:
Kate Langley Bosher published this novel in 1910, with Harper and Brothers, in a Grosset and Dunlap edition, with a frontispiece by Frances Rogers. It is told by Mary Cary herself, an orphan at the Yorkburg Female Orphan Asylum, who insists that things do happen in an orphan asylum. Orphans, she says, are real children, much like children with mothers and fathers, though they give no parties and wear no truly Paris clothes.

Fifteen chapters follow Mary from an unthankful orphan through the coming of Miss Katherine, the stepped-on and the steppers, a Reagan ball, and a true miracle, to a real wedding. The title chapter, Mary, Frequently Martha, names her busy, serving spirit. Bosher writes a warm, funny story of a girl who learns gratitude and love, in a voice that young readers still find direct and winning.
16296-sketches-from-my-life-by-the-late-:
Admiral Hobart Pasha set down these memories near the end of his life, and friends put them in print after his death in 1887. The book moves from a rough start at sea to slave hunting off Africa, blockade running, a visit to Charleston, and the siege of Richmond. Later chapters follow him into the Turkish navy, the war with Russia, and sport in Turkey.

Much of it was dictated on the Riviera while he was ill, and the tone stays plain and frank throughout. He names ships and ports, recalls close calls, and sketches the men he served with. For readers who like sea tales told by a man who lived them, the book gives a full naval life in short, brisk chapters.
17451-sign-language-among-north-american:
Garrick Mallery wrote this comparative study of sign language among North American Indians, set beside that of other peoples and of deaf mutes. Its long list of pictures shows signs for affirmation and approbation in old Roman, Neapolitan, and North American Indian use, for negation in Dakota use, and for love in modern Neapolitan use. Groups, questions, thieves, marriages, and money all appear among the illustrated signs.

Readers get a pioneering work of gesture studies, arguing that sign systems across cultures can be compared like spoken tongues. Mallery's plates make the argument visible, sign by sign. The book remains a foundation text for the study of gesture and of Indian sign language.
18822-the-house-of-martha:
Frank R. Stockton published this novel with Houghton, Mifflin in 1891. Its narrator, an only grandchild raised by his grandmother, tells his story from her quiet village house. From her parlor window she watches the street, trusting that he always does what is right.

Chapters follow his year in Europe, his book of travel, and a Sicilian love story, with a listener, an under-study, and a plan of seclusion along the way. Genoa, a sandbar, a floating grocery, and a distant topsail mark his wanderings, while Tomaso, Lucilla, and Sylvia people his tale. Stockton mixes gentle humor with romance, letting a traveler's book grow out of meetings, letters, and unfinished work.
19-the-song-of-hiawatha:
Henry Wadsworth Longfellow built an American epic from Ojibway legends gathered by Henry Rowe Schoolcraft. The Song of Hiawatha follows its hero from childhood to farewell in twenty-two cantos. Its steady trochaic beat made it easy to recite and remember.

Hiawatha learns the ways of forest and water, woos Minnehaha, and faces famine and loss. Chapters cover fasting, fishing, sailing, picture-writing, and the coming of white men. The poem closes with his departure as a new age arrives. Its popularity shaped how generations pictured Native stories, for better and worse.
24917-mariucha:
Benito Perez Galdos wrote Mariucha, a comedy in five acts, in this school edition prepared by S. Griswold Morley for Heath's Modern Language Series in 1921. The Spanish text comes with an introduction, notes, and a vocabulary for students.

Morley's life of Galdos notes that the author was born at Las Palmas in 1843. He studied law at Madrid without liking it, and turned from failed stage plays to novels before returning to drama. In Mariucha, Maria faces shame over letters her father, the Marques, pressed her to write in his straitened state. The edition suits students reading classic Spanish drama in the original.
26774-alcohol-a-dangerous-and-unnecessar:
Mrs. Martha M. Allen, superintendent of the Department of Medical Temperance for the National Woman's Christian Temperance Union, published this temperance book at Marcellus, New York, in 1900. Its subtitle promises how and why, with what medical writers say. Allen argues that alcohol is a dangerous and unnecessary medicine, and gathers doctors' opinions written in response to her letters of inquiry.

Chapters treat the Woman's Christian Temperance Union against alcohol as medicine, alcohol as a producer of disease, temperance hospitals, and the effects of alcohol upon the human body. Later chapters cover alcohol as medicine, alcohol in pharmacy, diseases and their treatment without alcohol, and alcohol and nursing mothers. Doctors quoted condemn alcohol for tubercular patients, saying it lowers resistance and leaves the person more open to disease.
27299-nothing-to-say-a-slight-slap-at-mo:
Nothing to Say, a slight slap at mobocratic snobbery, belongs to the Doesticks books, advertised as the funniest works in existence from Rudd and Carleton. The volume gathers the satires of Q. K. Philander Doesticks, Perfect Brick, whose letters were copied, quoted, and laughed over wherever they were lent.

Companion titles include Doesticks, What He Says, the compilation of his original letters, Plu-ri-bus-tah, a song by no author, and The Elephant Club, by Doesticks and Knight Russ Ockside. The verse spares neither the spirit of cant nor popular humbug and vulgar rant, in mid-century American comic satire.
32426-a-synopsis-of-the-north-american-l:
E. Raymond Hall's Synopsis of the North American Lagomorpha surveys rabbits, hares, and pikas of North America. It was published by the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History in volume five, number ten, pages 119 to 202, on December 15, 1951. With sixty-eight figures in the text, the synopsis gives the systematic treatment specialists need: names, ranges, characters, and relationships among lagomorph groups.

Hall, chairman of the museum's editorial committee, wrote for a series exchanged with learned societies, universities, and libraries. The paper's Latin-1 text marks male and female symbols and preserves bold, italic, and small-cap type from the original. It remains a standard reference for mammalogists studying North American lagomorph taxonomy and distribution.
34259-hunting-dogs-describes-in-a-practi:
Oliver Hartley teaches night hunting and gun dog work in a Harding handbook from Columbus, Ohio, held under rights from 1909. Full title lines promise training, handling, treatment, and breeds for night sport and daylight gun work alike. Plates show coon hounds, wolf hounds, and the fruits of a night hunt.

Part one covers night hunting, the coon dog, and training for skunk, opossum, mink, wolf, squirrels, and deer in turn. Part two turns to picking, care, and breeding of dogs, plus their ailments in full. Part three weighs still trailers against tonguers and the dog on the trap line. Part four sorts the family by breed, from fox hounds and beagles to pointers, setters, and Airedales.
35578-the-empty-sleeve-or-the-life-and-h:
The Empty Sleeve is the memoir of Henry Meacham, a Union soldier who lost his right arm, sold for his own benefit. Meacham says the lost arm shuts him out of most work, and that he writes to support his wife.

The narrative begins at the outbreak of the rebellion, with Meacham working as a carriage-maker in Russell, Massachusetts. Twice the examining surgeons rejected him; at the third attempt he was accepted, and his heart beat with joy. He sailed from Boston harbour with wistful glances back at home, and joined Company E of the Thirty-second Massachusetts Volunteers at Culpeper, Virginia, sixty miles from Washington. The memoir promises a plain soldier's account of the Army of the Potomac and the hospital, told by a man whose wound is the reason the book exists.
35993-the-history-of-don-quixote-de-la-m:
Cervantes wrote the tale of Don Quixote, and the form here, revised for plain reading, came out in London in 1848. A sketch of the life and works of the author stands at the front. The knight sets out in quest of bold deeds, is dubbed at an inn, and meets with mishap at each turn.

High points in the chapter list take in the charge at the windmills and the stay in the Sierra Morena. A curate and a barber plot to bring the knight home, and fair Dorothea joins their plan. Talk, song, and tales told on the road fill out a book long held as a crown of prose fiction.
37421-the-life-and-times-of-kateri-tekak:
Ellen Walworth published The Life and Times of Kateri Tekakwitha with Peter Paul at Buffalo in 1891. Copyright rests in 1890, and the years 1656-1680 stand under the title. She dedicates the book to her uncle Clarence Walworth, rector at Albany. Her preface tells how he first set her on this untried theme.

Kateri, an Indian girl raised in forest villages, won the name Lily of the Mohawks. Genevieve of New France was a second title the records gave her in honor. Walworth hunted Jesuit manuscripts at Montreal and papers at the Hotel Dieu for facts. Mohawk Valley places tied to her childhood and baptism guide the research throughout. Piety and local history fill a devoted life.
38000-bridge-its-principles-and-rules-of:
Elwell wrote a full guide to the card game of bridge, put out by Charles Scribner and Sons in New York in 1906. Bridge here is the early form of the game played by four hands with a pack of fifty two cards. Elwell first sets out how to cut for seats, deal, score tricks and honours, and win a rubber of three games.

Later parts teach how to declare a trump or play with no trump, how to bid, lead, and read a hand. Worked sample hands show the rules in play. The book ends with the club code of bridge laws, so home and club players could settle disputes by one shared standard.
46321-the-spell-of-the-heart-of-france-t:
Andre Hallays wrote a travel book on the towns and great houses near Paris. The book came out in 1920 with the Page Company. It starts with a scene at Fontainebleau from a famed French novel. Hallays uses the scene to name the charm of old homes.

He says old houses and gardens hold a scent of past ages. Those who know French history feel that charm most strongly. The first full stop on the tour is Maintenon and its great house. Readers get lore, art, and quiet praise for a rich region.
50188-the-invisible-foe-a-story-adapted-:
Louise Jordan Miln made The Invisible Foe, a story adapted from the play by Walter Hackett, printed in New York, copyright 1918 and 1920. A motto of three words stands at the front: blind, blind, blind. The tale falls in four books: the children, the dark, the quest, and the light. The first book opens out of doors with three children, each at a pastime.

Stephen lies on his stomach in a bed of moss, chin in palm, watching a bird's flight hungrily. Hugh sits against the big oak making a chain of blossoms. Helen plays by herself. Stephen is always watching birds fly. His uncle Richard once caned him for opening a cage and losing Helen her pet canary, all because he wanted to see just how it flies. It was worth more than a few smacks, Stephen said after.
52263-the-twilight-of-the-idols-or-how-t:
Friedrich Nietzsche's The Twilight of the Idols, with The Antichrist bound in, came out in Anthony Ludovici's translation in 1911. The volume is the sixteenth of the complete works in English, the first complete and authorised translation, edited by Oscar Levy and published by Foulis of Edinburgh and London. Notes to Zarathustra and the eternal recurrence fill the back.

Ludovici's preface dates the Twilight to the end of summer 1888, written in a few days at Sils Maria and finished on the third of September. It first bore the title Idle Hours of a Psychologist. The contents run from Maxims and Missiles through The Problem of Socrates and The Four Great Errors, to Things the Germans Lack and a closing word on what Nietzsche owed the ancients.
52668-making-over-martha:
Making Over Martha, by Julie M Lippmann, was printed at New York by Grosset and Dunlap, from a copyright of 1913. Martha Slawson sits at her machine, stitching white cloth for dear life while drifts of it pile at her feet. Her husband Sam comes in and asks what garment she makes. It is no garment: it is a motto, Hail to the Chief, in big yellow letters on white. She means to string it over the drive for a home crowd.

Mr and Mrs Ronald are due back from a year-long wedding tour, and Martha keeps their house. Sam hints Hail to the Bride would fit; she says no, a wife of a year is no bride, and the groom must not be left in the cold. Home fans get warm, sly wit from a sharp housekeeper.
53140-chickamauga-and-chattanooga-battle:
Chickamauga and Chattanooga Battlefields is handbook number twenty five of the National Park Service. Sullivan wrote it, and the Government Printing Office issued it in nineteen fifty six. It guides visitors to the national military park in Georgia and Tennessee. The price was twenty five cents from the Superintendent of Documents.

The history opens with the wartime weight of Chattanooga and east Tennessee. Rosecrans's Tullahoma campaign and the march to Chickamauga follow in short chapters. The two day battle of September eighteen sixty three is told phase by phase. Then comes the siege of Chattanooga and Grant's lifting of it in November. Orchard Knob, the battle above the clouds, and Missionary Ridge crown the account. A guide to the park, its roads, and its monuments closes the handbook.
58940-the-wolf-demon-or-the-queen-of-the:
Albert W Aiken spins a frontier tale in a dime novel issued by Beadle and Adams at New York in 1878. The story sold for ten cents as number forty-nine in Beadle's New York Dime Library. A prologue sets the scene by moonlight in the forest on the banks of the Scioto.

A frightened deer dashes across a moonlit glade, and a Shawnee warrior steals after it on noiseless feet. Storm clouds cross the moon, and night noises fill the greenwood as the hunt begins. The Shawnee, painted and fringed in deer skin, is drawn as one of nature's noblemen. Readers get dime novel frontier writing at full stretch, with the Kanawha country, its tribes, and its dangers ahead.
59328-modern-copper-smelting-being-lectu:
Donald Levy's Modern Copper Smelting, published by Griffin at London in 1912, prints his Birmingham University lectures greatly extended. Levy was assistant lecturer in metallurgy at Birmingham. An introduction covers the history, uses, and properties of copper. The frontispiece shows the converter flame through the stages of bessemerising copper matte: the slagging stage, the white metal stage, and the blowing to blister. Seventy-six illustrations accompany the text.

The preface says the lectures rest on study at the best organised smelters and refineries in the United States, where Levy spent considerable time. He aims at a compact volume on principles, with working practice from personal observation, a gap on the British side of the Atlantic. Lists of references close each lecture. Levy acknowledges Doctor Peters, whose classical volumes raised copper smelting to a science, among his sources.
59691-emin-pasha:
Plehn's life of Emin Pasha, translated from the German by George Upton for McClurg at Chicago in 1912, belongs to the Life Stories for Young People series. Upton's preface calls Emin the father of the Equatorial Provinces. A scientist devoted to zoology and botany, he kept up his studies through hardship, blindness, and neglect by the Khedive. Treacherous Arabs murdered him while he studied his plants and birds. Twenty chapters follow the slave question, the Mahdist advance, Casati's adventure, and Stanley's relief expedition.

The preface weighs the friction between Emin and Stanley. Emin was the quiet, cautious scholar who trusted the Soudanese and governed by mild measures. Stanley was the bold man of action, with little patience for slowness. Later chapters cover the mutiny, the march to Zanzibar, and Emin's return to the heart of Africa. Five illustrations accompany the text.
59770-the-plays-of-roswitha:
The Plays of Roswitha is an English translation of six medieval Latin dramas. Christopher St John made the translation, issued in 1923. Cardinal Gasquet wrote the introduction. Roswitha was a nun of Gandersheim in the tenth century. Her six short plays are named in the contents. Gallicanus, Dulcitius, and Callimachus come first.

Abraham, Paphnutius, and Sapientia complete the set. The translator lists the Latin editions behind the work. Conrad Celtes printed the plays first in 1501. Help came from a Benedictine superior and a Lyons scholar. Gasquet notes the plays reach English here for the first time. A closing note treats how they might be acted. Roswitha is the first known woman dramatist of Europe. Her saints' tales in play form drew on Terence's craft.
60438-chile-and-her-people-of-to-day-an-:
Nevin Winter describes Chile and Her People of To-day for Page at Boston in 1912, with photographs by the author. His subtitle promises the customs, character, amusements, history, and advancement of the Chileans, plus their country's resources. Companion volumes on Cuba, Panama, Argentina, Brazil, Guatemala, and Mexico front the book.

Seventeen chapters run from The Country and The West Coast through Vale of Paradise to the City of Saint James, Santiago under its old name. Later chapters treat the granary of the republic, the backbone of the continent, and an unconquerable race. History closes the tour: the struggle for independence, the Nitrate War, and civil war and its results. Present conditions and future possibilities end the account, with appendices and index.
61511-the-political-songs-of-england-fro:
Political Songs of England gathers songs from the reign of John to Edward the Second. An editor translated each song and set the rendering after its text. A transcriber's note explains signs for yogh, eth, and thorn in the type. Bracketed numbers in the text refer to line numbers of each song. The last song, on the evil times of Edward the Second, lacks a translation.

Various readings and glossaries sit within some songs in the original. Those helps stay in place, since they key to set line numbers above. Verse in Norman French, Latin, and early English voices politics of old. Barons, kings, taxes, and wars echo through rhymes once sung aloud. Scholars of medieval England mine the set for the mood of the streets.
61937-a-prose-english-translation-of-har:
A Prose English Translation of Harivamsha renders the Sanskrit appendix to the great epic literally into English prose. Manmatha Nath Dutt edited and published it at Calcutta in 1897. Dutt also translated the Ramayana, the Mahabharata, and several of the Puranas into English.

A long contents list shows the matter. A prelude leads to the primeval creation and the origin of men in the birth of Daksha. The story of Vena and Prithu, the origin of the earth, the ages of Manu, and the division of time follow. Chapters then trace the offspring of the sun and of Vaivaswata Manu, the tales of Satyavrata and Sagara, and the lore of the Pitris and the fruits of funeral offerings. The birth of the moon and the account of Pururava come later in the line of kings.
67937-the-song-of-tiadatha:
The Song of Tiadatha is a long narrative poem by Captain Owen Rutter, writing under a pen name, first printed at Salonica in January 1919. Fisher Unwin of London issued the British edition from 1920. The poem tells the story of a soldier of the Salonica army in the First World War.

The publishers note that the tale was common to very many members of that army. Only those who belonged to the British Salonika Force, they warn, can appreciate it to the full. Rutter dedicated the poem to his colonel, in memory of days in Wiltshire, France, and Macedonia. The verse follows the manner of a famous American song of an Indian hero. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
69787-the-splendour-of-asia-the-story-an:
Adams Beck tells the story and teaching of the Buddha in The Splendour of Asia, published by Dodd, Mead in New York in 1926. Beck dedicates the book to Ellery Sedgwick, who inspired its writing, and a Gandhara Buddha at Hoti-Mardan fronts the volume. Four parts carry the life and doctrine forward.

Part one opens with the words Thus have I heard, then sets Kapila in northern India in spring, nearly two thousand five hundred years ago. The Himalayas rise above the city, home of Indra, Surya, and Chandra in the telling, while the river Rohini runs below. Kapila, birthplace of the Perfect One, lies in the great kingdom of Kosala, peopled by the Sakya clan.
71196-the-book-of-martha:
The Book of Martha, by the Honourable Mrs Dowdall, came out in London in 1913 with a front plate by Augustus John. Its twenty-three short chapters treat the daily round of a kept house. Cooks, housemaids, tradesmen, job gardeners, doctors, children, charwomen, butlers, and dressmakers all pass in turn. Christmas, house-moving, shopping in London, and foreign travel fill out the list.

The first chapter owns that the book should by rights bear Ruth's name, since the author's servant held her house, her tradespeople, and her free time in her hands for thirty years. Ruth has now left, and the author writes in a small act of revolt to keep one thing her own. The tone is dry and fond, and the book gives a clear view of how a well-run Edwardian home rested on the work of one trusted maid.
72402-the-klygha:
Fyfe wrote this strange tale of shared minds for Amazing Stories' December 1963 issue. Schelling drew its plates. Its tag holds the theme whole: it is a considerable talent, to be able to use the minds of other beings to see for you, to talk for you. It is also a considerable risk.

It is hard, the tale opens, to be made a server by a being from outside the herd. It is hard to remember who is who; another is inside the head. The Klygha dreams to wake the cat. What is sleep? Why is a cat? The cat is not the herd-mind, yet the Terrans serve it, with food, with tickles. It does not work or hunt, and their minds are many where the Klygha's is one. Fyfe tells the puzzle from inside the guest mind.
73117-names-and-places-in-the-old-and-ne:
George Armstrong compiled this index of names and places in the Old and New Testament and Apocrypha, with their modern identifications. Charles Wilson and Major Conder revised the work. It was printed in London in 1889 for the Committee of the Palestine Exploration Fund. The preface lists the sources, from the survey memoirs of Palestine to Smith's Bible Dictionary.

The Old Testament index holds upwards of 1150 names of places in the Holy Land, Mesopotamia, Edom, Sinai, and Egypt. The New Testament index holds 162 names, of which 144 are known, 10 uncertain, and 8 not identified. Some 290 Old Testament places still wait to be fixed on the ground. Marks show which identifications rest on the survey itself.
77250-the-wisdom-of-the-apocrypha:
An anthology of the Apocrypha in the Wisdom of the East series. John Murray published it at London in 1910. L Cranmer-Byng edited the series as a whole. C E Lawrence wrote this volume's introduction. The texts come from the Revised Version, printed by permission. Space forced cuts, and a note owns them.

The Wisdom of Solomon opens the selections. Love righteousness, ye judges of the earth, it begins. Ecclesiasticus follows for the second half. The last nine chapters of Wisdom were spared as historical illustration. Some chapters of Ecclesiasticus also fell to the knife. Edward Frampton designed the cover. The series aimed to bring Eastern wisdom literature to general readers in small volumes.
79608-the-spoiled-buddha:
Helen Waddell wrote a play in two acts, printed in Dublin and London in 1919. The Ulster Theatre produced it at the Grand Opera House in Belfast in February 1915. A Buddhist priest speaks the prologue. The play tells of the Buddha in the days before he became a god.

Binzuru, his favorite disciple, might have risen as high as his master. Then he saw a woman pass by, desired her beauty, and fell from grace. Act one stands in the sacred grove five hundred years before Christ. Act two jumps to the temple court at Asakusa in Japan in the present day. Only a face painting pause parts two thousand four hundred years on stage.
8213-three-years-in-tristan-da-cunha:
K. M. Barrow, wife of the Reverend J. G. Barrow, missionary clergyman on Tristan da Cunha, wrote this account of three years on the remotest inhabited island in the world. With thirty-seven original illustrations from photographs and a map. The book aims to give a simple and true description of daily life among a very small community cut off from the rest of the world. Its language is largely that of letters to a sister and of Barrow's journal, with use of the official Blue Book and the Africa Pilot.

Barrow describes island routines, storms, ships, births, and burials, without literary pretence. The result is an intimate record of isolation and community. For readers of travel and island life, it is a rare, first-hand portrait of Tristan before modern communications, told by a woman who lived it.
8324-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-24-cant:
Lovers speak, seek, and find each other in the Canticle of Canticles, the Douay-Rheims name for the Song of Songs. A young woman and her beloved praise each other's beauty in images from vineyards, gardens, spices, and the hills of Lebanon, parting and reuniting in verses of longing. No plot holds the poems together, only desire and delight.

Jewish tradition reads the song for Passover, and Christians have read it as Christ's love for the church, but the poems also stand as plain love poetry. Challoner's revision from the Latin Vulgate gives the verses in older Catholic wording, with the Latin title kept. It is the Bible's most sensual book, and one of its shortest.
ayesha:
H. Rider Haggard brought back his deathless queen Ayesha in this book of 1905. Its full name is Ayesha: The Return of She. Fans had waited near twenty years since She first came out to learn her fate. Leo's quest, and hers, had held readers since that first wild book.

Leo Vincey, who loved Ayesha in the first book, is drawn to her new form in the hills of Asia. The tale ranges through storms, cults, and the fire of her strange rebirth in full stretch. Haggard gives his occult romance its most vast and wild form in this long tale.
britannica-1911-agrapha:
Agrapha means unwritten things in Greek. The name covers sayings ascribed to Jesus outside the Gospels. Such utterances survive in other early documents. Acts quotes one: it is more blessed to give than receive. Paul's letters preserve several more sayings. The Logia found at Oxyrhynchus in 1897 joined them. Those papyrus finds renewed scholarly interest greatly. Two examples show the range of material.

One saying promises the weak salvation through the strong. It comes from the Apostolic Canons, about A.D. 300. The second calls the world merely a bridge. Cross over it, it says, do not dwell on it. Missionary Alexander Duff found that saying in Arabic. It was inscribed on a mosque gateway at Fatehpur Sikri. Collections began with Cotelerius in the seventeenth century.
britannica-1911-ahmed-tewfik-pasha:
Ahmed Tewfik Pasha, a Turkish diplomat born in 1845, is noticed in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of Ismail Hakki Pasha. He began his career in the army, then left the service in 1862 while still a young man. Four years later he entered diplomacy instead, and was employed at various European capitals.

Steady postings carried him upward through the Ottoman foreign service. He became minister at Athens in 1883, the empire's resident envoy to Greece. The next year he rose to ambassador in Berlin, one of the great postings of the day. In 1896 he reached the top of his profession at home. He was appointed minister for foreign affairs, the office the entry gives in Turkish as Kharijie Naziri.
britannica-1911-ali-pasha:
Ali Pasha (1741–1822), the Turkish ruler of Iannina nicknamed Arslan, the Lion, grew up bent on revenge. He was born at Tepeleni, an Albanian village below the Klissura mountains, into a Toske family. His forebears, hereditary beys of the place, lost their lands after nearby chiefs slew his father.

His mother Khamko, a woman of strong character, raised and led a band of brigands herself. She trained her son in her own fierce spirit, aiming him at payback and at winning back the lost estate. Ali learned fast. Scores of tales praise the cunning he showed as a young brigand chief in the hills. By a bold trick he seized Tepeleni again and settled scores with his foes. The long entry then tracks his years of rule and the struggle for Parga, which its people gave to the British in 1814 rather than let him take it.
britannica-1911-batalha:
Batalha, a town of Portugal in the district of Leiria, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica as a place known for one great building. The town, with 3858 people in 1900, stands on the site of old Canoeira. Its name, the Portuguese word for battle, and the monastery's name both recall the fight at Aljubarrota in 1385. There John I of Portugal beat John I of Castile and kept his kingdom free.

Dominicans built the monastery of Santa Maria da Victoria, St Mary of the Victory, in golden-brown stone cut like marble. It runs about 500 feet from north to south. Inside are a royal cloister, a chapter-house, and the Founder's chapel. That chapel holds the tombs of John I, Queen Philippa, and Prince Henry the Navigator. Kings after them lie in the round royal tomb house, famed for fine carved stone.
britannica-1911-buddha:
Buddha is the title given to the founder of Buddhism. In Europe the name means the last historical Buddha. His family name was Gotama. This long 1911 Britannica article examines his life. He was the son of Suddhodana, a chief of the Sakiya clan. That clan was one of India's republican tribes.

The article opens with a warning about legend. Miraculous tales gather around every religious founder, it says. Some scholars once called the Buddha a pure myth. The entry rejects that view firmly. A basis of truth lies under the tales, it argues. The article then sets out his birth and early circumstances. It places them in the 6th century B.C. It weighs the oldest records against the later legends. Its aim is an intelligent history of the man. Readers get both the tradition and the criticism of it.
britannica-1911-chaetognatha:
Chaetognatha is the name for a small group of clear, mostly sea-dwelling animals, and this 1911 Britannica entry sets out what is known of them. The group was named by R. Leuckhart and holds just three genera, Sagitta, Spadella, and Krohnia, with few species in all. Yet the animals swarm in vast numbers, at times so thick that the sea surface seems stiff with them. Rough seas drive them down into deeper water for safety.

The body is shaped like a small torpedo, most kinds only one to three centimetres long, with side flanges and a round, swollen head. It falls into three parts, head, trunk, and tail, split by two cross walls. The head carries a hood that can be pulled back, plus curved chitin hooks and short rows of spines at its sides.
britannica-1911-chickasha:
Chickasha is a city and the county-seat of Grady county, Oklahoma, near the Washita river, about 45 miles south-south-west of Oklahoma City. Its people rose from 3,209 in 1900 to 10,320 in 1910, a fast growth in a new state. Three railways serve the city, the St Louis and San Francisco, the Chicago, Rock Island and Pacific and the Oklahoma Central. The city is the trade centre of a very fertile part of the Washita Valley.

Corn, cotton, fruits, vegetables and live-stock are the chief products of that valley land. Manufactures in the city include flour, cotton-seed oil, lumber, furniture and farm implements. Chickasha was founded in 1892, only seven years before it was chartered as a city in 1899. Fertile soil, rail links and new town growth explain the sharp rise in numbers that the entry records.
britannica-1911-covilha:
Covilhã is a town of Portugal in the district of Castello Branco, once part of the province of Beira. It stands on the east slope of the Serra da Estrella, on the Abrantes to Guarda railway. Its people numbered 15,469 in 1900. The town has often been likened to a clutch of swallows' nests. Those nests cling to a rugged granite mountain side in the image.

Houses crowd in the shape of an amphitheatre on that slope. They look down on the river Zezere and its wild valley from 2,180 feet. More than 4,000 workers make saragoça in the town. That coarse brown cloth is worn by the peasantry across Portugal. The village of Unhaes da Serra lies six miles west. Its sulphur springs and baths draw note in the entry. Cloth, height and springs form the town's whole mark.
britannica-1911-elisha:
Elisha, a Hebrew name meaning “God is deliverance,” was in the Bible the disciple and successor of Elijah. The hosted file holds several articles together; this entry is the Elisha article within it. Elijah chose him during the reign of Ahab, and he lived on until the reign of Joash. His career thus spanned nearly sixty years.

The entry contrasts the two prophets sharply. Elijah is the prophet of the wilds, rugged and austere, a messenger of vengeance whose miracles are mostly works of wrath. Elisha is the prophet of city and court, a messenger of mercy whose miracles are mostly works of healing. The entry instances the healing of Naaman and the feeding of a hundred men with twenty loaves. It also warns that the narrative order is confused and incomplete, so no firm chronology can be drawn.
britannica-1911-esterhazy-of-galantha:
Esterházy of Galántha is a noble Magyar family, treated at length in this 1911 Britannica article. Its origin is traced, with some doubt, to Salamon of Estoras, whose sons split their lands in 1238. The first man of the family to stand clear in history was Ferencz Zerházy, who took the name Esterházy when made lord of Galántha.

His sons founded several houses of the family. The line that holds the largest place in Hungarian history came from Miklós Esterházy (1582-1645). Born a Protestant, he turned to the Catholic faith and became a pillar of that cause in both church and state. He married a rich widow and gained vast estates, and in 1622 he acquired Fraknó. Kings raised him step by step with titles and honours, including the order of the Golden Fleece.
britannica-1911-fuad-pasha:
Fuad Pasha (1815-1869), Turkish statesman, was the son of the poet Izzet Molla. Educated at the medical school, he began as an army surgeon, then about 1836 moved into the foreign ministry. He served as embassy secretary in London, on missions in the principalities and at St Petersburg in 1848, and as special commissioner in Egypt in 1851.

That year he first became minister for foreign affairs, a post he held four more times and still held at his death. In the Crimean War he commanded troops on the Greek frontier with noted bravery. He was Turkish delegate at the Paris conference of 1856 and grand vizier in 1860 and 1861. His settlement of affairs in Syria after the massacres of 1860 is singled out for praise. Known for bold, quick decisions and ready wit, he leaned toward England in policy. He died at Nice in 1869.
britannica-1911-garrucha:
Garrucha is a seaport in the south east of Spain, on the Mediterranean coast at the mouth of a river. The 1911 Britannica entry gives its town count at the turn of the age, a few thousand souls. An old fort guards its port, which gives safe berth to large ships.

Small as it is, and with no rail link, the town ships a large trade. It is the natural outlet for a rich district of farms and mines round it. Lead, silver, copper, iron, grass for rope, and fruit all pass through its port. Sea ships and a swarm of small coast boats crowd in, most of them British or Spanish. In ten years the worth of its trade, in and out, grew threefold.
britannica-1911-gastrotricha:
Gastrotricha, in the 1911 Britannica, is a small group of tiny freshwater animals. They live among rotifers and protozoa at the bottom of ponds and marshes, hiding in algae and sphagnum and eating debris and infusoria. Their size runs from about a sixtieth to a three-hundredth of an inch, and they swim by bands of fine hairs called cilia.

The article describes the scaled skin, bristles, mouth, toothed throat and simple stomach in close detail, with a labelled figure of Chaetonotus maximus. It covers nerves, sense hairs, eggs and the little-known male system. Zelinka's classification closes the piece, splitting the group into fork-tailed and plain-tailed sub-orders. Some forty to fifty species are reckoned described, and the entry stresses that the group's kinship to other animal phyla is unclear.
britannica-1911-geisha:
Geisha is a word for the professional dancing and singing girls of Japan, and a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives the term its strict sense. The word is of Chino Japanese origin and means a person of pleasing accomplishments. In loose use it is often applied to the women of the Shin Yoshiwara, a quarter of Tokyo. The entry is careful to keep the two apart.

Training of the true geisha includes lessons in dancing, the entry says. That training begins often as early as her seventh year. When her apprenticeship ends, she contracts with her employer for a set term of years. She can seldom reach independence except by marriage, in this account. A tax of two yen a month fell on the singing girls. Apprentices paid a fee of one yen a month.
britannica-1911-gray-elisha:
Elisha Gray is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was an American worker in electric craft born in Ohio in eighteen thirty five. He laboured as a carpenter and read science books on his own time. Five years of college study and teaching honed that self taught base.

The entry tells how he won patents for telegraph tools in his early years. His tests sent tones and tunes of music along a wire. On one famed day he filed a claim for a talking wire tool. A rival claim by Bell had been filed just hours before on that day. Courts upheld the rival, but Gray won high praise and honours abroad.
britannica-1911-halakha:
Halakha is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a part of Jewish law. The word means literally rule of conduct. It names the rabbinical development of the Mosaic law. With the haggada, it makes up the Talmud and Midrash. As the haggada is the poetic element, so this is the legal one. It arose from a clash between two parties. 

The Pharisees strove to prove those traditions came from scripture. Many attempts were made to codify the halakha over time. The Great Rules of Simon Kayyara came in the ninth century. That work rested on letters of the Babylonian school heads. Jacob Alfassi produced another code in his lifetime. The Strong Hand of Maimonides followed in 1180. Joseph Qaro's Table Prepared came in 1565. For its practical scope and clarity, that book won wide use. It became the universal handbook of Jewish life.
britannica-1911-hiawatha: Hiawatha, whose name means he makes rivers, was a legendary chief (c. 1450) of the Onondaga tribe of North American Indians. Indian tradition credits him with forming the League of Six Nations, known as the Iroquois. In his miraculous side he stands as the embodiment of human progress and civilization. He teaches agriculture, navigation, medicine and the arts, and by his magic defeats the powers of nature that war against man. The short entry sits at the head of a hosted file that also holds other entries.
britannica-1911-hobart-pasha:
Hobart Pasha was born Augustus Charles Hobart-Hampden in 1822 and died in 1886. The 1911 Britannica life presents him as both English captain and Turkish admiral. He was born in Leicestershire, third son of an earl of that land. In 1835 he joined the Royal Navy as a young lad. He served off Brazil to help stamp out the slave trade there.

In 1855 he fought in the Baltic as captain of the Driver. He took part in the attacks on Bomarsund and on Abo. He left the navy in 1862 with the rank of post captain. Love of risk then drew him to run the blockade for the South. He ran war goods to Charleston eighteen times and came back with cotton.
britannica-1911-hrosvitha:
Hrosvitha, properly Hrotsuit, was an early medieval dramatist and chronicler. Her work formed part of the literary stir by which the age of Otto the Great sought to match the age of Charles the Great. She was a nun of Gandersheim, not to be confused with a learned abbess of the same name, dead half a century before her.

The younger Hrosvitha was born in all probability about 935. Before 959 she entered the Benedictine nunnery of Gandersheim, a house kept for ladies of German birth and much favoured by the Saxon dynasty. In 959 Gerberga, niece of Otto, became her abbess and teacher. If it is true that she sang the praises of the three Ottos, she lived near the century's close. The long article takes up her plays in Latin after Terence, her legends in verse, and her chronicles of the Ottonian house.
britannica-1911-ibrahim-pasha:
Ibrahim Pasha, an Egyptian general who lived from 1789 to 1848, has a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He is most often called the son of Mehemet Ali, pasha of Egypt, though some call him an adopted son. He was born at Kavala in Thrace, the native town of his father. As a youth of sixteen he was sent as a hostage to the Ottoman admiral.

When Mehemet Ali was upheld as pasha and had beaten an English force, Ibrahim was let return to Egypt. In 1813 his father went to Arabia to war on the Wahhabis, and Ibrahim held command in Upper Egypt. He crushed the last strength of the Mamelukes in that time. In 1816 he took command of the Egyptian forces in Arabia from his brother Tusun. That campaign lasted two years and ended with the Wahhabis destroyed as a power in the land.
britannica-1911-jugurtha:
Jugurtha was king of Numidia, the unlawful son of Mastanabal and grandson of Massinissa. After his father's death his uncle Micipsa raised him beside his cousins Adherbal and Hiempsal. He grew up strong, handsome, and keen, a skilled rider and adept in war. Micipsa, fearing him, sent him to Spain in 134 B.C. with a Numidian force under Scipio Africanus.

In Spain he became a favourite with Scipio and the Roman nobles, some of whom put into his head the thought of taking the whole kingdom. When Micipsa died in 118 B.C., his will joined the three princes in the rule of Numidia. The plan failed at once. Jugurtha had Hiempsal murdered and drove Adherbal out. Rome split the kingdom and gave Jugurtha the richer western half, leaving Adherbal the sands of the east.
britannica-1911-katha:
Katha is a district in the northern division of Upper Burma, with an area of 6994 square miles. Of that area, 3730 square miles form the former separate state of Wuntho. The Upper Chindwin, Bhamo, and Myitkyina districts bound it on the north. The Kaukkwe River and the Irrawaddy bound it on the east, the Ruby Mines district and Shwebo on the south.

Three ranges of hills run through the district, the Minwun, the Gangaw, and the Mangin. They split the three main rivers, the Irrawaddy, the Mèza, and the Mu. The Minwun range runs north to south and for much of its length parts the Katha district proper from the old Wuntho state. Its mean height is 1500 to 2000 feet. The Gangaw range keeps close to the right bank of the Irrawaddy for much of its course.
britannica-1911-kinorhyncha:
Kinorhyncha, an isolated group of minute sea animals, is the subject of a science entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The group holds a single genus, Echinoderes, named by Dujardin, with some eighteen species. They occur in mud and on sea weeds at the bottom of shallow seas, below low water mark. There they feed on organic debris, the entry says.

The body is enclosed in a stout cuticle, drawn out in places into spines and bristles. Two rings of spines round the proboscis and two tail spines stand out most clearly. The body is divided into eleven segments, and the thrust out proboscis into two. The mouth opens at the tip of that proboscis, which can be pulled back into the body. It leads through a short tube to a muscular gizzard lined with thick cuticle. The entry sets out the salivary glands, stomach, and other parts in detail.
britannica-1911-menasha:
Menasha is a place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It describes a city in Wisconsin in the United States, at the north end of a large lake. The city stands where the lake flows out into a river. Bridges link it to a twin town across the water.

The entry gives counts for four census years and notes good water power. Mills make paper, wood goods, cloth goods, leather, and boats. An island at the river mouth serves as a summer resort. French and English trade posts stood on the site in early times. The town was settled for good in eighteen forty eight and won a charter later.
britannica-1911-midhat-pasha:
Midhat Pasha (1822-1884) was a Turkish statesman, and his reforming career is traced in an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Son of a civil judge at Constantinople who favored reform, he was trained for administration. At twenty-two he became secretary to an official in Syria. Posts in finance and on the grand council followed.

The entry tells how his enemies got him sent to settle revolt and brigandage in Rumelia, a task thought impossible, and how his drastic measures succeeded startlingly. He restored order in Bulgaria in 1857. As governor of Nisch his reforms so impressed the sultan that he was charged with framing a scheme for the whole empire, later known as the law of the vilayets.
britannica-1911-osman-pasha:
Osman Pasha, who lived from 1832 to 1900, was a Turkish field marshal in a 1911 Britannica life. He was born at Tokat in Asia Minor and trained at the military academy in Constantinople. He joined the cavalry in 1853 and served in the war with Russia in Wallachia and the Crimea. Guard posts and campaigns in Lebanon and Crete brought him steady rise.

He won note at the taking of a convent fort in Crete and gained rank fast. Yemen service in 1871 was followed by corps command at Widin in 1876. There he beat Serbian forces twice and took two towns that autumn. The entry builds toward the defence that would make his name world famed.
britannica-1911-rewa-kantha:
Rewa Kantha, a group of native states in India, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is a political agency under the government of Bombay. The tract stretches about one hundred and fifty miles, from the plain of Gujarat to the hills of Malwa. It takes its name from the Rewa river, which it crosses.

The agency holds sixty-one separate states, many under direct British rule. Only one of them, Rajpipla, ranks as truly important. Five more are graded as second-class states. The whole covered nearly five thousand square miles at the census of 1901. Its people then numbered 479,065, down by more than a third in ten years. That fall is laid to famine in the decade. Many of the people belong to the Bhil and Koli tribes. The agent lives at Godhra, where he also serves as a district collector.
britannica-1911-riaz-pasha:
Riaz Pasha, born about 1835, was an Egyptian statesman of Circassian family stock. The 1911 Britannica entry says little is known of his early life in any detail. Until Ismail became viceroy in 1863 he held a lowly place in service. Ismail saw in him a hard worker with a strong will and raised him.

To his dismay the khedive found Riaz honest and fiercely his own man as well. When debt forced a commission of inquiry, Riaz was named its vice president. He filled that post with credit but not to the khedive liking at all. Later Ismail had to name him to office under a new constitutional pose.
britannica-1911-said-pasha:
Said Pasha, born about 1830, was a Turkish statesman called Kuchuk. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows his many turns at the top. He first edited a Turkish newspaper in his early career. On a new sultan accession he became first secretary.

Said helped that sultan draw all power into his own hands. Posts as interior minister and governor of Brussa followed in turn. In 1879 he reached the grand vizier post at last. The entry calls him an old school man of narrow views. He fought the spread of foreign weight in Turkey. Four more spells as grand vizier came under that sultan. In 1896 he fled to the British embassy for shelter. A revolution in 1908 briefly raised him to the top again.
britannica-1911-shemakha:
Shemakha is a town article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a place in Russian Transcaucasia, in the Baku district, some seventy miles west of Baku town. The article puts its people at about twenty thousand, made up of Tatars, Armenians, and Russians. Shemakha had once been the chief town of the khanate of Shirvan, and the Roman writer Ptolemy knew it as Kamachia.

The history that follows is rough. In the middle of the sixteenth century the town held an English trade post. In 1742 Nadir Shah of Persia took and wrecked it, then built a new town of the same name some miles away. In time the old site was rebuilt, and Russian forces took the town more than once, in 1723 and again in 1795. The entry gives a clear sense of a trade town caught between empires.
britannica-1911-wardha:
Wardha is a town and district of British India, in the Nagpur division of the Central Provinces, as this 1911 Britannica article describes them. Both take their name from the Wardha river. The town stands south-west of Nagpur by rail and had 9,872 people in 1901. It was laid out in 1866, soon after the district was first formed, and is a weighty centre of the cotton trade.

The district covers 2,428 square miles. It is hilly in the north, cut by spurs from the Satpura range, and its middle part holds three peaks, of which Jaitgarh at 2,086 feet is the highest. Many small streams run from that cluster of hills to the Wardha river. Other streams, the Dham, Bor, and Asoda, flow down the length of the district toward the south-east, and the land to the south spreads out flat.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agrapha:
Agrapha, a name J. G. Korner first used in 1776 for Jesus's Sayings surviving outside the canonical Gospels. After Alfred Resch chose the expression as his learned work's title on these Sayings in 1889, its technical meaning was generally accepted. The entry considers the Agrapha's limits first, their genuineness criteria second, and the list of those probably authentic.

Three conditions govern the Agrapha. They must be Sayings, not discourses; Sayings of Jesus; and not contained in the canonical Gospels. Being mere Sayings, they exclude long Jesus sections in the Didascalia and Pistis Sophia. Being Sayings of Jesus, they exclude sayings in religious romances such as apocryphal Gospels and Acts or Christ's Letter to Abgar. They also exclude Scripture passages ascribed to Jesus by mere oversight.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apocrypha:
Apocrypha covers writings that claim authorship by biblical figures, and this long article sorts them by origin rather than by the misleading split into Old and New Testament groups. Works once called apocryphal but now counted as patristic literature, such as the Shepherd of Hermas, the Letter of Barnabas, and the Didache are treated elsewhere. Jewish apocrypha broadly match the Old Testament set, and Christian apocrypha the New Testament set.

The survey runs through Jewish apocalypses, legendary tales, psalms and prayers, and philosophy. Then it covers Jewish works with Christian additions, then Christian gospels, Pilate literature, acts of apostles, doctrinal works, epistles, and apocalypses. The entry is a map for readers who meet a strange gospel or lost psalm. It shows where it came from, when it was written, and why it never entered the canon, the accepted list of Scripture.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bertha:
Bertha, a name borne by several holy women, receives a grouped entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia, with five singled out for notice. First stands Bertha, Queen of Kent, a Frankish princess who married the pagan King Ethelbert and brought her chaplain Liudhard to Canterbury. There she restored a Roman-era church dedicated to St. Martin.

Her influence smoothed the way for St. Augustine's mission of 596, and Pope Gregory wrote to her in 601. Other Berthas in the entry include abbesses and queens of later centuries. The piece is a small gallery of women who carried faith into courts and convents.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-birtha:
Birtha, a titular see of Osrhoene, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Probably the same as Birejik on the Euphrates, some sixty-two miles west of Edessa, its Aramaic name means castle, and ancient writers call it just that. A second name, Macedonopolis, claims Alexander the Great as founder by legend.

Proof that Birtha and Macedonopolis are one see comes from Nicaea's subscription lists, where the Syriac and Arabic form matches the Greek and Latin name. The entry is a short identification puzzle solved by comparing council lists across languages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-kateri-tek:
Blessed Kateri Tekakwitha, the Lily of the Mohawks, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in 1656 at Ossernenon or Gandaouge, she died at Caughnawaga in Canada in 1680. Her mother was a Christian Algonquin captured by the Iroquois, saved by Tekakwitha's father, and mother also of a son.

Smallpox at about four killed her parents and brother, and aunts and a chief uncle adopted her. Baptised despite family opposition, she lived a life of prayer and penance, fleeing to the Christian village of Caughnawaga. The entry presents a young Mohawk woman whose holiness bridged two worlds.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canatha:
Canatha was a titular see of Arabia, named Kanatha, Kanotha, or even Kenetha on coins and in geographies, with its own era. It is certainly not Kanata, now Kerak, nor Maximianopolis, since Severus of that see and Theodosius of Kenatha sat together at Chalcedon in 451. Josephus first mentions it for a defeat of Herod by the Arabs, and Pliny and Ptolemy count it among the towns of the Decapolis.

In the old episcopal lists it answers to Bostra as suffragan, and one bishop is known, Theodosius, from 449 to 458. Today it is El-Qanawat, northeast of Bostra at about 4,100 feet, amid woods. Its magnificent ruins run 4,800 feet long, among them a Roman bridge, a rock-hewn theatre, a nymphaeum, an aqueduct, and two temples.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eliseus-elish:
Eliseus, or Elisha, was the prophet who followed Elijah, and this entry follows his wonder-working career. On Mount Horeb, Elijah learned that Elisha son of Shaphat was chosen as his successor. Elijah cast his mantle over Elisha as he ploughed with twelve yoke of oxen. Elisha killed the oxen, boiled their flesh on his plough wood, feasted with family and friends, and then followed his master.

After Elijah was taken up in a fiery chariot, Elisha parted the Jordan with the fallen mantle and won recognition at Jericho as heir to Elijah's spirit. He healed Jericho's waters with salt, and bears mauled boys who mocked him at Bethel. Later he multiplied a widow's oil to pay her debt, and he foretold both rain and victory for the allied kings against Moab. The entry shows a prophet whose miracles served the poor, the king, and the nation alike.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fray-antonio-:
Fray Antonio de la Calancha, an erudite Augustinian monk born in 1584 at Chuquisaca, now Sucre, in Bolivia, and dead on 1 March 1654. He wrote one of the great chronicles of colonial Peru. Both his parents were of Spanish blood, he studied at Lima, entered the Order of St. Augustine, and served successively as definitor, secretary of the province, and rector of the College of San Ildefonso. During the earthquake that ravaged Trujillo on 14 February 1619 he headed that city's convent, and later became prior at Lima.

His most important work, the Moralised Chronicle of the Order of St. Augustine in Peru, appeared in two bulky volumes in 1638 and 1653, now very rare, written in a ponderous style but full of valuable detail on the Indians of Peru and Bolivia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gabbatha:
Gabbatha is the Aramaic name for the place in Jerusalem where Pilate sat in judgment on Jesus. It appears only in John 19:13, beside the Greek name Lithostrotos. John calls the tongue Hebrew, as New Testament writers did, though the speech of Judea in that day was Aramaic. The entry weighs what the two names truly mean.

Lithostrotos means a mosaic pavement, the floor before Pilate's headquarters where his judgment seat stood. Gabbatha, by contrast, comes from a root meaning back or height, pointing to the rise of the ground itself. Scholars have tried to pin the spot to the Temple court, the Sanhedrin's meeting place, or a ridge behind the Temple, but none of these guesses holds. Only Pilate's seat there stands certain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gerrha:
Gerrha, a titular see in Augustamnica Prima suffragan of Pelusium under Alexandria, survives in geographers and bishops' lists. Pliny mentions the city, Eratosthenes says its district once lay underwater, and Strabo sets it between Pelusium and Mount Cassius. Hierocles in the sixth century places it in Augustamnica.

Lequien gives four bishops: Eudaemon, Pirosus, and Nilanmon at the fourth century's end and the fifth's start, and Stephen, who attended Chalcedon in 451. Marshes have since encroached on the land, and the abandoned city lies on the El-Arish road north of Pelusium. The entry's brevity suits readers tracing Egypt's lesser sees, ancient geography's shifting coast, and the councils' attendance lists.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hamatha:
Syria's Hamath, a titular see suffragan of Apamea, was capital of a Canaanite kingdom whose king Thou congratulated David on beating the king of Zobah. Solomon seems to have held it, Amos calls it Hamath the Great. Assyria seized it in the seventh century before Christ, while Macedonian rulers renamed it Epiphania for Antiochus Epiphanes.

As Epiphania it is best known in church records, with nine Greek bishops listed by Lequien, the first signing at Nicaea. Arabs took it in 639 and restored the old name as Hamah. Franks held it briefly in the twelfth century, the geographer Yakout was born there, and modern Hamah on the Orontes counts 45,000 people, about 10,000 of them Christians of several rites.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hroswitha:
Hroswitha, also spelled Roswitha and Hrotsvitha, was a celebrated nun-poetess of the tenth century, probably born between 930 and 940 and dead about 1002. Her name, read as mighty voice, explains her titles as the mighty voice and the Nightingale of Gandersheim. Probably of aristocratic birth, she entered Gandersheim convent in her earliest youth, then famed for asceticism and learning.

Her talents found wise cultivation under her teacher Rikkardis and then under Gerberg, Otto I's niece, and the most accomplished woman of her day, later her abbess. Gerberg fostered Hroswitha's muse in hopes of adding to God's glory. Little more is known of her outer life, but her writings, the first German poetess's work, are far better known, and the entry surveys them in detail.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maspha:
Maspha is the name of several biblical places, from Hebrew Mitzpeh and Mitzpah, meaning watch-tower, from the root watch or observe. The Septuagint writes Maspha, Massepha, and Massephat, the Vulgate Maspha and Masphath. It fits towns in commanding positions, like Crusading Belvoir, and almost always carries the article.

Maspha of Gilead is where Jacob, ratifying his compact with Laban, set up a stone pillar and called for stones, and where Israel later gathered against Ammon. Whether it matches Ramath ha-Mitzpeh or Ramoth Gilead cannot be decided. Maspha of Benjamin, assigned by Joshua, draws rival identifications: Nebi Samwil, Shafat by Guerin, Tell en-Nasbeh, and el-Bireh, judged perhaps best for water, northerly position, and road. Maspha of Judah lies in the Shephelah between Delea and Jechtel. Near Hermon lies a Land of Maspha, and David fled with his parents to Maspha of Moab from Adullam.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-moses-bar-kep:
Moses Bar Kepha, one of the most celebrated Jacobite bishops and writers of the ninth century, was born at Balad about 813. He died at ninety in 903. An anonymous Syriac biography survives in a Vatican manuscript, excerpted by Assemani. It tells how he became a monk, then bishop of Beth-Ramman, Beth-Kionaya and Mossoul on the Tigris under the name Severus. For ten years he served as patriarchal visitor of Tagrit.

His numerous works span theology, philosophy, controversy, exegesis and liturgy. The chief ones are a commentary on both Testaments often quoted by Bar Hebraeus, a treatise on predestination and free will in the British Museum, and a commentary on Aristotle's Dialectics. They include a five-book Hexameron at Paris, a Tractatus de Paradiso, and writings on the soul and the sacraments. He was buried in the monastery of Saint Sergius near his native city.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-omaha:
Omaha, a Nebraska diocese covering all the state north of the South Platte, spans 52,996 square miles. Jesuits visited Nebraska Indians from about 1838, the Holy See carved the Rocky Mountain vicariate from Saint Louis in 1851, and Nebraska became its own vicariate in 1857.

James O'Gorman, a Trappist from Tipperary who helped found New Melleray in Iowa, became first resident vicar apostolic in 1859. The entry follows the diocese through railroads, farming towns, and immigrant parishes to its schools, hospitals, and clergy at the century's turn. James O’Gorman took the Trappist habit at Mount Melleray in 1839 and was ordained in 1843.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ramatha: The Roman Curia suppressed Ramatha, a titular see in Palestine, in 1884. It was never a bishop's see in the proper sense. In the Middle Ages the crusaders set up the Diocese of Lydda and Rama. Its titular was generally called Bishop of Rama, meaning Ramlet, a town near Lydda but more populous than Lydda itself. Later that history was forgotten, and separate titular sees of Lydda and of Rama, or Ramatha, came into being. The mistake has since been discovered and put right.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-maelrub:
Maelrubha, abbot and martyr and founder of Abercrossan, was born in 642 and died on 21 April 722. Descended from Niall, king of Ireland, through his father Elganach, he was born in County Derry and educated at Bangor. At thirty he sailed from Ireland to Scotland with monks, travelled for two years, chiefly in Argyll, and founded about half a dozen churches.

He then settled at Abercrossan, now Applecross, in the west of Ross, and built his chief church and monastery among the Picts. From there he journeyed west to Skye and Lewis, east to Forres and Keith, and north to Loch Shin, Durness, and Farr. On the journey he was martyred by Danish vikings, probably at Teampull, nine miles up Strath-Naver from Farr, and buried near the River Naver beneath a rough cross-marked stone.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saxe-coburg-a:
Saxe-Coburg and Gotha, a Saxon-Thuringian duchy pair, covers 751 square miles: Coburg at 216 and Gotha at 541, split by Saxe-Meiningen and a Prussian strip. In 1910 the land held 257,208 people, with 3,897 Catholics, about two per cent, in 1905. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia explains a union that kept its halves apart.

Joined in 1826, the two duchies still kept separate constitutions, diets, and internal rule, even for religion and schools, meeting jointly only for specified business. Besides the split itself, race kept them apart: Gotha's people were Saxon stock, Coburg's Frankish. Crown-land differences also shaped taxation. The entry traces both duchies from the Wettin divisions to their modern constitutional life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sodom-and-gom:
Sodom was a city of Pentapolis, joined with Gomorrha, Adama, Seboim, and Bala, later called Segor. The five cities stood in the country about the Jordan, though their exact location is unknown. Josephus placed Segor at the south end of the Dead Sea, while later scholars proposed sites north and south of the sea and on the Lisan peninsula.

For the unnatural sins of their inhabitants, Sodom, Gomorrha, Adama, and Seboim were destroyed by brimstone and fire from the Lord out of heaven. Since then their names stand for impenitent sin, and their fall for a proverbial display of God's just wrath. The Septuagint's word katastrophe probably bred the mistaken idea that the destruction brought great upheavals of earth and even formed the Dead Sea.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-agatha:
St. Agatha ranks among the most venerated virgin martyrs of Christian antiquity, put to death at Catania in Sicily for steadfast profession of faith. This entry admits uncertainty over which persecution claimed her. While accepting as probably rooted in ancient tradition the later legendary life that places her martyrdom under Decius between 250 and 253.

Historic certitude, it stresses, attaches only to the martyrdom itself and to public veneration from primitive times. The Hieronymian Martyrology and the fifth- or sixth-century Carthaginian Martyrology both record her on 5 February. And by the sixth century Venantius Fortunatus was already praising her among celebrated Christian virgins, a fame the entry traces to its earliest sources.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-hereswitha:
Hereswitha, sister of Hilda of Whitby, became a nun at Chelles after her husband fell in battle. Daughter of Hereric and Beorhtswith, she married Aethelhere, king of East Anglia, and bore him two sons, Aldwulf and Alfwold. The Liber Eliensis wrongly calls her wife of Anna, Aethelhere's elder brother, a mistake the entry corrects firmly. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 places her widowhood at the battle of Winwaed in 655.

After her husband's death she entered Chelles abbey, then in the Paris diocese, and remained there until her life's end. Her feast wanders through the calendars: Stanton gives 3 September, the second English Martyrology 20 September, the first edition and Ferrari 23 September, Bucelinus 1 December. The Bollandists propose discussing her cult on that December day. The entry preserves a queen turned nun, dated four ways.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-martha:
Martha of Bethany, sister of Mary and Lazarus, appears in Luke and John in strikingly similar portraits. Luke 10:38-42 and John 11 and 12 alone mention her, her Aramaic name appears in a Nabataean inscription from Puteoli, now in Naples Museum, dated A.D. 5, and in a Palmyrene inscription of A.D. 179, where Greek gives Marthein. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 weighs the Gospels' geography with care.

John places Mary, Martha, and Lazarus at Bethania, while Luke seems to imply they lived at one time in Galilee, though he names no town. That town may have been Magdala, which, supposing Mary of Bethania and Mary Magdalene the same person, would explain the name Magdalene. John 11:1 seems to suggest the family had moved, and Luke may have displaced his chapter 10 incident. The likeness between Luke's and John's Martha is, the entry says, very remarkable.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tryphon-respi:
Martyrs whose feast the Latin Church observes on 10 November. Tryphon, said to have been born at Kampsade in Phrygia, tended geese as a boy. During the Decian persecution he was taken to Nicaea about 250 and put to death after converting the heathen prefect Licius, though fabulous stories are woven into his legend.

He is patron of gardeners in the Greek Church, which keeps his feast on 1 February. About 1005 the monk Theodoric of Fleury made Respicius his companion in story. The relics of both, with those of the Palermo virgin Nympha, were kept at Rome's Hospital of the Holy Ghost until Pius V moved them to Saint Augustine's in 1566. Leo VI, the Philosopher, delivered a eulogy upon Tryphon, and the Greek Church counts him patron of gardeners.
deuterocanonical-books-of-the-bible-apoc:
The hosted text gathers the deuterocanonical books, called the Apocrypha in English Bibles. It uses the classic English long printed with the King James Bible. The books include the two books of Esdras, Tobit, and Judith. They also include the Greek additions to Esther, the Wisdom of Solomon, Sirach, and Baruch. The Letter of Jeremiah follows. So do the Song of the Three Holy Children, Susanna, Bel and the Dragon, and the Prayer of Manasses. Both books of the Maccabees close the set.

These writings come from the last centuries before Christ. They were written in the Jewish world under Greek and Roman rule. Catholic and Orthodox churches count most of them as scripture. Most Protestant churches do not, but print them for study. Tobit's angel tale, Judith's daring rescue, and the Maccabees' revolt remain the most read.
doe-osti-17030342-implementation-of-cont:
Hendrik Kohlwes of Los Alamos National Laboratory describes adding a damage model to the xRAGE simulation code in this report, issued September 29, 2026. xRAGE models radiation and fluid flow in extreme events. The added method, continuum damage mechanics, tracks how a material weakens as damage builds inside it, rather than treating strength as fixed.

Sections lay out the current strength calculation flow in the code, then the damage math, then a modified workflow that fits the model in. A one dimensional tension test serves as the worked example, with figures showing model behavior under varied settings. A discussion weighs what the change means for later strength modeling in the code.
doe-osti-2584612-k-3-refractory-corrosio:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory test report by Tongan Jin, Long Q. Le, Nathan L. Canfield, and colleagues including J. D. Vienna records how K-3 refractory survives molten glass. K-3 is a candidate material for lining glass melters, the furnaces that vitrify radioactive waste, and a melter lining that corrodes fast ends campaigns early. Coupons were immersed in a static melt of HAL24M2 glass at set depths, following the laboratory's standard corrosion protocol.

The volume is a results record: glass fabrication, the corrosion test method, and then the measured attack on the coupons, section by section. An appendix photographs every coupon after exposure. A second appendix presents micro-CT imaging, which reveals corrosion below the surface that calipers cannot see. For the Hanford vitrification program, choosing a refractory is a bet placed on data exactly like this: how much material the glass eats, and where it eats deepest.
doe-osti-2588164-on-the-cfl-limit-for-st:
Michael Schneider, Jane Pratt, and Alexx Perloff of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory wrote this technical report, LLNL-TR-2008697, dated August 18, 2025. All three work in the laboratory's Astronomy and Astrophysics Analytics Group. Their subject is a stability limit that governs explicit time stepping for equations used in optimal control. Through a recent recasting, it reaches quantum mechanics too.

The Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation of optimal control can be rewritten as a Schrödinger equation, as Schneider and colleagues showed in 2022. Implicit solvers such as Crank-Nicolson are unconditionally stable and conserve mass or energy, but explicit Euler schemes are cheaper per step. For them, the Courant-Friedrichs-Levy limit caps the time step. The report derives that limit and the role of the potential's size. Its central image is an effective velocity: the CFL number compares the solution's physical speed with the speed the grid can resolve.
doe-osti-3000942-lllinois-storage-corrid:
Curt Blakley, Zohreh Askari, Yaghoob Lasemi and co-workers at the University of Illinois issue this pre-drilling site assessment. It is DOE-UIUC-31892-2, dated 5 November 2025, for the Illinois Storage Corridor CarbonSAFE project. Beside the Prairie State Generating Company coal plant near Marissa, Illinois, a stratigraphic test well will probe whether carbon dioxide can be stored underground for good. The target is at least 50 million metric tons.

Two reservoirs lead the plan, the Potosi Dolomite and the St Peter Sandstone, capped by the Maquoketa Group as seal. The assessment mines existing Illinois Basin data for rock structure, thickness maps, shallow groundwater and nearby old wellbores, and forecasts the depths drilling will meet. No known structural feature threatens the reservoir or its caprock. The coming well will return core, fluid samples, in-situ tests and geophysical logs to settle the site's fitness.
doe-osti-3001003-illinois-storage-corrid:
Sallie Greenberg and Jung Sung of the University of Illinois write the outreach plan for the Illinois Storage Corridor. It is report DOE-UIUC-31892-3, issued 6 November 2025, under agreement DE-FE0031892, with Roland Okwen as principal investigator. The corridor would gather carbon dioxide from industry across Illinois and store it underground. Two anchor sites frame the plan: the One Earth Energy ethanol plant in the north, and the Prairie State coal plant in the south. Together they would capture over 8.6 million tons a year at full build out.

Carbon storage is poorly understood by the public, and opposition born of unfamiliarity can kill projects. The plan organises engagement in four parts: communication, stakeholder analysis, engagement actions and environmental justice. It identifies who must be reached, from landowners to local officials, and sequences the outreach. As a planning document, it sets the framework rather than reporting engagement already done.
doe-osti-3012696-illinois-storage-corrid:
Koenig, John, Christopher Korose, and Carl Carman of the University of Illinois wrote this technical report, issued January 10, 2026, as subtask 5.5 of the Illinois Storage Corridor CarbonSAFE Phase III project. The corridor would store carbon dioxide in deep salty rock formations at two Illinois hubs, one near One Earth Energy in east-central Illinois and one near the Prairie State Generating Company campus. Project partners emit over 6.5 million tonnes of carbon dioxide a year.

The report works through the policy, legal, and permitting ground the project must cross. Federal Class VI well permits govern injecting carbon dioxide underground, with drinking water protection as the central concern. Property rights in underground pore space, pipeline siting and safety rules, public engagement, and post-injection site care each get detailed treatment.
doe-osti-3020412-illinois-storage-corrid:
Illinois Storage Corridor CarbonSAFE Phase III deliverable DOE-FE0031892-11, issued February 16, 2026, is a permitting plan for storing captured carbon dioxide underground in Illinois. The authors come from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, the Illinois State Geological Survey, and project partners. Before any injection well can operate, it needs a UIC Class VI permit from regulators, and this plan maps how the project will earn one.

The plan schedules pre-permitting meetings with regulators, including the U.S. EPA, which joined the project kickoff in November 2020. It then outlines each permit application's contents: site characterization, area of review and corrective action, well construction, financial responsibility, monitoring, plugging, and post-injection site care. Data handling follows EPA guidance through the Geologic Sequestration Data Tool. The document is a roadmap, written so each storage site's application arrives complete.
doe-osti-3022837-a-comparison-of-gpu-acc:
ANL report ANL/ALCF-25/3, by Alexander Gardner, Chunheng Zhao, Saumil Patel, and colleagues, benchmarks GPU-accelerated multiphase flow solvers on the Polaris supercomputer at the Argonne Leadership Computing Facility. Two-phase flows, gas and liquid moving together, underpin applications from nuclear cooling to chemical processing, and this first part of the comparison sets up the contenders and their mathematical formulations.

Two codes receive detailed treatment. FluTAS enforces strict incompressibility and applies surface tension as a continuum force at a sharp interface, using the MTHINC method to move the interface with the flow. ImExLBM takes a lattice Boltzmann route to the same governing physics. Laying the formulations side by side, including how each handles gravity and volume fractions, sets up the performance measurements the series exists to deliver.
doe-osti-3023975-investigating-the-impac:
Qi Zhang of the University of California, Davis, closes award DE-SC0022140 with this final technical report on how water in the air changes organic aerosol. Organic particles affect sunlight, cloud formation, and how readily droplets form. Much of that material is secondary, made in the air from gases, and the pathways are still not fully pinned down, which leaves climate models uncertain.

Using observations from the ARM user facility and the ASR program, the project tracked aqueous-phase chemistry in cloud, fog, and aerosol water. Such processing quickly makes highly oxidized, low-volatility compounds, plus light-absorbing brown carbon. Analyses of water-soluble aerosol and fog water found spectral markers of this chemistry, including organic acids and nitrogen-bearing compounds, and organic nitrogen stood out as a useful tracer.
doe-osti-3625675-robust-and-high-through:
National Laboratory of the Rockies report NLR/TP-2800-100208, dated August 2026, closes CRADA CRD-21-21472 with Shell Global. Justin Sluiter and Zofia Tillman were the lab contacts, and the report date is March 2, 2026. The work ran from July 2022 to April 2025. It built standard lab methods for wet manure feedstocks and for digestate, the leftover from anaerobic digestion that yields renewable natural gas.

Shell built and ran two pilot dry digesters on dairy manure mixed with corn stover. Smaller bags of wheat straw, corn stover, and energy grasses were buried in the piles for extra sample types. Stirred tank reactors ran in parallel for comparison. The methods were checked for full mass closure and for clear, repeatable measures of key parts. The same samples then fed near-infrared models meant for fast checks at working plants. Faster, trusted testing could raise output of low-carbon gas from wet waste.
doe-osti-3874817-mixed-materials-icf-sim:
Charged particle tracking joins mixed-material fusion capsule simulations in Los Alamos report LA-UR-26-27818, issued August 31, 2026.
